thinking-s1.title: Same facts, different wording

plot.label: Bar graph of the percent of participants who chose the surgery: 80% when told 90% survive, 40% when told 10% die (invented data)

thinking-s1.html: Sixty adults read about a surgery and decided whether they would choose it. A computer randomly assigned each person to one of two versions. Half (30) read that 90% of patients survive the surgery; the other half (30) read that 10% of patients die from it. The graph shows the percent in each version who chose the surgery.

thinking-s2.title: The candle problem and the box of tacks

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether seeing an object in its usual role makes it harder to use it in a new way. Participants had to attach a candle to a wall so it could burn without dripping wax on the table, using a candle, a book of matches and a box of thumbtacks. The solution is to empty the box, tack it to the wall and use it as a shelf.
study.participants: 48 high school juniors from two schools took part with written parental permission and their own agreement. Each was told they could stop at any time.
study.method: Students were randomly assigned to one of two groups of 24. In the full-box group, the tacks were given inside the box. In the empty-box group, the tacks were given beside the empty box. Each student worked alone, and a researcher timed how many minutes the student took to reach the solution, up to 10 minutes.
study.results: The empty-box group solved the problem in an average of 2 minutes; the full-box group took an average of 6 minutes, and 7 of its students did not solve it within 10 minutes.
study.discussion: The researchers concluded that seeing the box as a container made it harder to see it as a shelf.

items.q: Both versions give the same survival odds. Which concept explains why the choices differed?
options: The framing effect
The availability heuristic
Functional fixedness
The gambler's fallacy

why.correct: The facts were identical; only the wording changed. A gain frame ("90% survive") led to more choices of surgery than a loss frame ("10% die"). That is the framing effect.
options: Right: The facts were identical; only the wording changed. A gain frame ("90% survive") led to more choices of surgery than a loss frame ("10% die"). That is the framing effect.
The availability heuristic is judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Nothing here asked people to recall examples.
Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in its usual use. No object or problem to solve is involved.
The gambler's fallacy is expecting a run of outcomes to "even out". The participants made one choice from one description.

items.q: In the "10% die" version, 12 of the 30 people chose the surgery. Check the graph: what percent is that?

why.correct: $\frac{12}{30} \times 100 = 40\%$, the height of the second bar.

mistakes.why: 20% divides by all 60 people. Only 30 read the "10% die" version, so divide by 30.
12 is the count of people, not a percent. Divide by 30 and multiply by 100.

items.q: Why can the researchers conclude that the wording caused the difference in choices?
options: Sixty adults is enough people to prove any result is true
Chance alone decided which version each person read, so the groups were alike except for the wording
The people chose freely, so their answers show their real preferences
Both versions were read on a computer screen in the same lab room

why.correct: Random assignment spreads people's other differences evenly across the two groups, so the wording is the only systematic difference. That allows a cause-and-effect claim.
options: Sample size alone never proves a cause. What allows the causal claim is that the wording was manipulated and people were randomly assigned.
Right: Random assignment spreads people's other differences evenly across the two groups, so the wording is the only systematic difference. That allows a cause-and-effect claim.
Free choice does not rule out other explanations; random assignment is what makes the groups comparable.
Keeping the setting the same helps, but without random assignment the groups could still differ in other ways.

items.q: Which concept best explains why the full-box group took longer?
options: The representativeness heuristic
Divergent thinking
Functional fixedness
Priming

why.correct: With the tacks inside, students saw the box only as a container, its usual function, and were slow to see it as a shelf. That is functional fixedness.
options: The representativeness heuristic judges how likely something is by how well it matches a prototype. Students were not judging likelihood.
Divergent thinking is producing many possible solutions, the opposite of being stuck. It describes what helped, not what slowed students down.
Right: With the tacks inside, students saw the box only as a container, its usual function, and were slow to see it as a shelf. That is functional fixedness.
Priming is earlier exposure making a related idea come to mind faster. It could help solve problems, but the slowdown came from seeing the box only as a container.

items.q: What was the operational definition of problem-solving performance in this study?
options: Whether the tacks came inside or beside the box
How creative each student felt during the task
The number of students who were in each of the groups
Minutes a student took to reach the solution, up to 10

why.correct: An operational definition states how the study measured the variable: the timed minutes to solve, with a 10-minute limit.
options: That is the independent variable, the condition the researchers changed.
A feeling is not what the study measured. It timed how long students took.
The group size (24) describes the sample, not the measure of performance.
Right: An operational definition states how the study measured the variable: the timed minutes to solve, with a 10-minute limit.

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary describe, and how was it applied?
options: Informed assent and permission: parents gave written permission and each student agreed to take part
Debriefing after deception: students were told the true purpose after a cover story
Random assignment: each student had an equal chance of being in either group
Confidentiality: names were replaced with code numbers before analysis

why.correct: For minors, researchers get a parent's informed consent and the young person's own agreement (assent). The summary says both were obtained.
options: Right: For minors, researchers get a parent's informed consent and the young person's own agreement (assent). The summary says both were obtained.
The summary describes no deception and no debriefing, so this safeguard cannot be credited to the study.
Random assignment is a design feature that supports cause and effect. It is not an ethical guideline.
The summary never mentions how names were handled, so this is not a safeguard it describes.

items.q: A student in the full-box group first tried to melt wax to glue the candle to the wall, then kept trying versions of that same idea. Which concept describes this second problem?
options: The sunk-cost fallacy
Mental set
Convergent thinking
The framing effect

why.correct: A mental set is the tendency to keep using an approach that worked before, or that came to mind first, even when it is not working.
options: The sunk-cost fallacy is continuing because of what you have already invested (money, time). Nothing suggests the student kept going because of time already spent.
Right: A mental set is the tendency to keep using an approach that worked before, or that came to mind first, even when it is not working.
Convergent thinking narrows to one best answer. It is a normal step in problem-solving, not getting stuck on one failing approach.
The framing effect is about how wording changes a choice. The task wording was the same for everyone.

items.q: Asked to picture a "bird", most people imagine something like a robin, not a penguin. A robin is the bird category's what?
options: Algorithm
Heuristic
Prototype
Mental set

why.correct: A prototype is the best, most typical example of a concept. People judge membership by comparing new cases with it, which is why a penguin feels like a less "birdy" bird.
options: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, not an example of a category.
A heuristic is a mental shortcut for judging or solving. The robin is the example, not the shortcut.
Right: A prototype is the best, most typical example of a concept. People judge membership by comparing new cases with it, which is why a penguin feels like a less "birdy" bird.
A mental set is a habit of approaching problems one way. It is not the typical example of a category.

items.q: A child calls every four-legged animal at the farm a "dog". Later she learns that cows and horses are different, and she makes new categories for them. What is the second step?
options: Assimilation
Priming
Functional fixedness
Accommodation

why.correct: Changing a schema, or making a new one, to fit information that does not fit the old one is accommodation.
options: Assimilation is fitting new things into an existing schema, which is the first step (calling every animal a dog).
Priming is earlier exposure making a related idea come to mind faster. It does not describe changing a category.
Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in its usual use. It is not about building categories.
Right: Changing a schema, or making a new one, to fit information that does not fit the old one is accommodation.

items.q: Ana needs to find a misspelled name in a list of 500, so she checks every name, one by one, against the class roster. Which strategy is she using?
options: An algorithm
A heuristic
Divergent thinking
A mental set

why.correct: Checking every case in order is a step-by-step procedure that is slow but guaranteed to find the error if she follows it. That is an algorithm.
options: Right: Checking every case in order is a step-by-step procedure that is slow but guaranteed to find the error if she follows it. That is an algorithm.
A heuristic would be a shortcut, such as checking only the names that look odd. Ana checks every name.
Divergent thinking is generating many different ideas. Ana is following one fixed procedure.
A mental set is sticking with an old approach that may not fit. Nothing suggests her method is wrong for the job.

items.q: After a week of news stories about a plane crash, Jordan decides to drive across the country instead of flying, though driving is far more dangerous per mile. Which concept explains his judgment?
options: The representativeness heuristic
The availability heuristic
The sunk-cost fallacy
Functional fixedness

why.correct: Vivid, recent crash stories come to mind easily, so Jordan judges flying as more dangerous than it is. That is the availability heuristic.
options: Representativeness is judging by how well something matches a prototype. Jordan is judging by how easily examples come to mind.
Right: Vivid, recent crash stories come to mind easily, so Jordan judges flying as more dangerous than it is. That is the availability heuristic.
The sunk-cost fallacy is sticking with something because of what you have already invested. Jordan has invested nothing.
Functional fixedness is about seeing objects only in their usual use, not about judging risk.

items.q: Told that a quiet man loves poetry, most people guess he is a classics professor rather than a truck driver, even though there are far more truck drivers. Which concept explains the guess?
options: The availability heuristic
The framing effect
The representativeness heuristic
Mental set

why.correct: People judge by how well he matches their prototype of a professor and ignore how common each job is. That is the representativeness heuristic.
options: Availability is about how easily examples come to mind. The guess comes from matching a description to a prototype.
The framing effect is about wording a choice as a gain or a loss. Nothing is framed that way here.
Right: People judge by how well he matches their prototype of a professor and ignore how common each job is. That is the representativeness heuristic.
A mental set is a habit of solving problems one way. This is a judgment of likelihood, not a problem-solving habit.

items.q: A roulette wheel has landed on red seven times in a row. Malik bets on black, sure it is "due". Which concept describes his error?
options: The sunk-cost fallacy
The availability heuristic
Priming
The gambler's fallacy

why.correct: Each spin is independent; past spins do not change the odds of the next. Expecting a streak to reverse is the gambler's fallacy.
options: The sunk-cost fallacy is continuing because of what you already spent. Malik's error is about predicting the next spin.
Availability is judging by examples that come to mind easily. Malik is reasoning about a streak, not recalled examples.
Priming is earlier exposure speeding up a related idea. It does not explain believing an outcome is "due".
Right: Each spin is independent; past spins do not change the odds of the next. Expecting a streak to reverse is the gambler's fallacy.

items.q: Priya has paid for a concert ticket. On the night she is sick and would rather stay home, but she goes anyway because "I already paid for it." Which concept explains her choice?
options: The sunk-cost fallacy
The gambler's fallacy
The framing effect
Mental set

why.correct: The money is spent whether she goes or not. Letting a past, unrecoverable cost drive a choice is the sunk-cost fallacy.
options: Right: The money is spent whether she goes or not. Letting a past, unrecoverable cost drive a choice is the sunk-cost fallacy.
The gambler's fallacy is about expecting random outcomes to even out. No chance event is involved.
The framing effect is a change in choice caused by wording. The ticket was not described two ways.
A mental set is a habit of solving problems one way. Priya is deciding whether to go, not solving a problem.

items.q: Students who first read a list including the word "ocean" are faster to recognize the word "wave" a minute later. Which concept explains this?
options: Accommodation
Priming
The framing effect
Convergent thinking

why.correct: Earlier exposure to "ocean" activated related ideas, so "wave" was recognized faster. That is priming, often without awareness.
options: Accommodation is changing a schema to fit new information. Nothing about the schema changed.
Right: Earlier exposure to "ocean" activated related ideas, so "wave" was recognized faster. That is priming, often without awareness.
The framing effect changes a choice through wording. There is no choice here, only faster recognition.
Convergent thinking narrows to one best answer to a problem. Recognizing a word is not problem-solving.

items.q: In a brainstorming session, Leo is asked to list as many uses for a brick as he can in two minutes. Which kind of thinking is the task measuring?
options: Convergent thinking
Functional fixedness
Divergent thinking
An algorithm

why.correct: Generating many different possible answers is divergent thinking, a key part of creativity.
options: Convergent thinking narrows to one correct answer, as on a multiple-choice test.
Functional fixedness would make it hard to think of new uses. The task measures the opposite.
Right: Generating many different possible answers is divergent thinking, a key part of creativity.
An algorithm is a fixed step-by-step procedure. There is no single procedure for listing uses.

items.q: After damage to her prefrontal cortex, a patient can still define words and do arithmetic but struggles to plan a meal, switch between tasks and stop herself from interrupting. Which abilities are most affected?
options: Prototypes
Perceptual constancy
Convergent thinking
Executive functions

why.correct: Planning, switching attention and controlling impulses are executive functions, which depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex.
options: Prototypes are typical examples of categories. Her knowledge of words is intact.
Constancy keeps objects looking stable in size, shape and color. Her trouble is planning and control, not perception.
She can still find single correct answers (arithmetic). Her trouble is organizing and controlling behavior.
Right: Planning, switching attention and controlling impulses are executive functions, which depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex.
